--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.node_connectivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute global node connectivity. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.node_connectivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute global node connectivity. title: >- [Graph.node_connectivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Compute global node connectivity. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute global node connectivity. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L79614-L79715){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.node_connectivity() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Node connectivity](../assets/graphs/node-connectivity.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two diamonds that share the hub node D, drawn in the accent color. Removing D alone disconnects the graph, so the node connectivity is 1, smaller than the edge connectivity of 2. The card shows the cut D and the value 1." width="100%"} Returns the minimum number of nodes whose removal disconnects the graph. This is the smallest local node connectivity over pairs of non-adjacent nodes. Only pairs that include one of the first `k + 1` nodes need checking, where `k` is the smallest value found so far, since a cut of `k` nodes must leave one of them out (Even, 1975). On a directed graph, "disconnected" means not strongly connected: some remaining node can no longer reach another along edge directions. A digraph that is only weakly connected therefore has connectivity `0`. Pairs are ordered (Even and Tarjan, 1975), because separating `v` from `u` can take fewer nodes than separating `u` from `v`. Self-loops and parallel edges don't change the result. Uses Menger's theorem: node connectivity equals the maximum number of node-disjoint paths. Implementation transforms the problem to max-flow. Time complexity: `O(k * V)` maximum flows, where `k` is the connectivity. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Minimum number of nodes needed to disconnect the graph. Returns `0` if already disconnected. Returns `n-1` for complete graph `K_n`. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~node_connectivity_between`) : The connectivity between two given nodes. [](`~edge_connectivity`) : The fewest edges whose removal disconnects the graph. [](`~all_node_cuts`) : Every smallest set of nodes whose removal disconnects the graph. [](`~k_components`) : The groups of nodes with at least a given connectivity. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A cycle falls apart only when two of its nodes are removed, while in the complete graph `K_5` every node but one would have to go: ::: {#83e5e0b6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec cycle = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(6) k5 = ec.Graph().add_full_graph(5) cycle.node_connectivity(), k5.node_connectivity() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (2, 4) ``` ::: ::: On a directed graph the nodes must still reach each other along edge directions. A one-way ring is broken by removing any one node, but with each edge doubled back the ring needs two: ::: {#12d90d27 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} pairs = [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A")] one_way = ec.Graph.from_edges(pairs, directed=True) both_ways = ec.Graph.from_edges( pairs + [(v, u) for u, v in pairs], directed=True ) one_way.node_connectivity(), both_ways.node_connectivity() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1, 2) ``` ::: ::: ### Closures that split the metro `metro()` is a made-up city's metro network. Closing a single station, such as Riverside, can split it, so its connectivity is 1. Its core of 15 stations, the largest biconnected block, needs two closures: ::: {#c565343b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} metro = ec.metro() core = max(metro.biconnected_components(), key=len) metro.node_connectivity(), metro.subgraph(core).node_connectivity() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (1, 2) ``` ::: ::: Closing Old Town and Northpark together is one way to split the core, cutting Westgate, Mill Lane and Hillcrest off from the rest: ::: {#3d5dfdd9 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} metro.plot( layout="pos", highlight=["Old Town", "Northpark"], label_by="label" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: With both closed, the core falls into two pieces, colored apart: ::: {#d3ec9b44 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} split = metro.subgraph(core) split.delete_node("Old Town").delete_node("Northpark") pieces = sorted(split.weakly_connected_components(), key=len) piece = {n: i for i, nodes in enumerate(pieces) for n in nodes} split.set_node_attrs("piece", piece).plot( layout="pos", color_by="piece", label_by="label", legend=False ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: [Connectivity and flows](../user-guide/connectivity.qmd#measuring-connectivity) explains why the connectivity of a whole network says little, and what is more informative.
